---
title: "LaTeX Accessibility Issues Checklist"
---

There are the common accessibility issues in LaTeX. They can be detected by PDF Accessibility Check tools.

## Structure {#l_structure}

### logical structure

When writing a LaTeX file, It's important to organize the content in a clear and logical order. Tools like tagpdf will tag the document with appropriate logical and semantic structure within the proper writing order.

Code
```latex
\section{} %first heading level
\subsection{} %second heading level
\subsubsection{} %third heading level
\paragraph{} %fourth heading level
\subparagraph{}
```

### Tagged structure {#access_issues}
Standard LaTeX doesn't automatically produce tagged PDFs that meet accessibility standards.A typical LaTeX PDF doesn't included information like "This is a heading" etc. so screen readers can't understand the logical structure of the document. We could address this issue by using tagpdf. tagpdf generates tag tree for your document. Click [tagpdf](#tagpdf) to see it's instructions and details.

## Color Contrast {#l_color}

In files generated using LaTeX, most of the time, color contrast meets accessibility standards. If you need to set your own colors, please refer to: [Colors in LaTeX](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Using_colors_in_LaTeX#Accessing_additional_named_colors)

## Alt Text {#l_alt}

In Latex, you can insert alternative text using `alt` inside `\\includegraphics`. And make sure to use tagpdf with it for accessibility.

``` latex
\includegraphics[alt={alt text}]{image.png}
```

### Use AI to help generate alt text

You can ask generative AI to help generate alt text for you!

Prompt: `Please generate alternative text for this image. It must follow the WCAG standard. Use the provided context or code if available. Keep it short and focused on the essential meaning of the image. Do not exceed the recommended character limit.`

## Accessible Math {#l_math}

To make sure math content meets digital accessibility standards:

Use correct LaTeX math syntax. Always write math using `\( ... \)` or `\[ ... \]` instead of faking it with text formatting. Screen readers rely on this structure.

And there are two ways to create accessible math content:

### tagpdf

When using tagpdf: Use the latest setup to correctly tag math formulas for PDF accessibility. See setup guide here: [tagpdf usage instruction](https://latex3.github.io/tagging-project/documentation/prototype-usage-instructions)

### Provide LaTeX math in HTML

When converting to HTML: Use tools like MathJax to render math correctly. This allows screen readers to detect and read equations. See [MathJax](https://docs.mathjax.org/en/latest/index.html)

Here are some resources about how to make accessible math through HTML:
[Accessible Mathematics](https://www.accessiblemath.info/accessible_math_documentation_page.html)

[Converting LaTeX to HTML: technical notes](https://richardzach.org/2023/07/converting-latex-to-html-technical-notes/)

[Accessible textbook in Math](https://richardzach.org/2025/03/accessible-open-textbooks-in-math-heavy-disciplines/)
